Don't be embarrassed — postpartum depression is common. Share your symptoms with your provider so that you and your provider can create a useful treatment plan. As part of your evaluation, your health care provider may do a depression screening, including having you fill out a questionnaire. Your provider may order other tests, if needed, to rule out other causes for your symptoms. Treatment Treatment and recovery time vary, depending on how severe your depression is and what your individual needs are. If you have an underactive thyroid or an underlying illness, your health care provider may treat those conditions or refer you to the appropriate specialist. Your health care provider may also refer you to a mental health professional. Baby blues The baby blues usually fade on their own within a few days to 1 to 2 weeks. In the meantime: * Get as much rest as you can. * Accept help from family and friends. * Connect with other new moms. * Create time to take care of yourself. * Avoid alcohol and recreational drugs, which can make mood swings worse. * Ask your health care provider about getting help from a health professional called a lactation consultant if you're having problems with producing milk or breastfeeding. Postpartum depression Postpartum depression is often treated with psychotherapy — also called talk therapy or mental health counseling — medicine or both. * Psychotherapy. It may help to talk through your concerns with a psychiatrist, psychologist or other mental health professional. Through therapy, you can find better ways to cope with your feelings, solve problems, set realistic goals and respond to situations in a positive way. Sometimes family or relationship therapy also helps. Examples of therapies used for postpartum depression include cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) and interpersonal psychotherapy. * Antidepressants. Your health care provider may recommend an antidepressant. If you're breastfeeding, any medicine you take will enter your breast milk. However, most antidepressants can be used during breastfeeding with little risk of side effects for your baby. Work with your provider to weigh the potential risks and benefits of specific antidepressants. * Other medicines. When needed, other medicines may be added to your treatment. For example, if you have postpartum depression that includes severe anxiety or insomnia, an antianxiety medicine may be recommended for a short time. Brexanolone (Zulresso) is the first drug approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration specifically for postpartum depression in adult women. Brexanolone slows the rapid drop of certain hormones after childbirth that may lead to postpartum depression. Potential serious side effects require a stay in a health care facility and monitoring by a health care provider while receiving the medicine through a vein over 60 hours. Because of this, the treatment is not yet widely available. Research continues on an oral medicine for postpartum depression with promising results. The medicine being studied works in a way similar to brexanolone. But it could be taken daily as a pill and may not have the same serious side effects. With appropriate treatment, postpartum depression symptoms usually improve. In some cases, postpartum depression can continue and become long term, which is called chronic depression. It's important to continue treatment after you begin to feel better. Stopping treatment too early may lead to a relapse. Postpartum psychosis Postpartum psychosis requires immediate treatment, usually in the hospital. Treatment may include: * Medicines. Treatment may require a combination of medicines — such as antidepressants, antipsychotic medicines, mood stabilizers and benzodiazepines — to control your signs and symptoms. * Electroconvulsive therapy (ECT). ECT is a procedure in which small electrical currents are passed through the brain, intentionally starting a brief seizure. ECT seems to cause changes in brain chemistry that can reduce the symptoms of psychosis and depression, especially when other treatments have been unsuccessful. But it can also result in something you might not expect — depression. Most new moms experience postpartum "baby blues" after childbirth, which commonly include mood swings, crying spells, anxiety and difficulty sleeping. Baby blues usually begin within the first 2 to 3 days after delivery and may last for up to two weeks. But some new moms experience a more severe, long-lasting form of depression known as postpartum depression. Sometimes it's called peripartum depression because it can start during pregnancy and continue after childbirth. Rarely, an extreme mood disorder called postpartum psychosis also may develop after childbirth. Postpartum depression is not a character flaw or a weakness. Sometimes it's simply a complication of giving birth. If you have postpartum depression, prompt treatment can help you manage your symptoms and help you bond with your baby. Products & Services * A Book: Mayo Clinic Guide to a Healthy Pregnancy * A Book: Mayo Clinic Guide to Your Baby's First Years Show more products from Mayo Clinic Symptoms Symptoms of depression after childbirth vary, and they can range from mild to severe. Baby blues symptoms Symptoms of baby blues — which last only a few days to a week or two after your baby is born — may include: * Mood swings * Anxiety * Sadness * Irritability * Feeling overwhelmed * Crying * Reduced concentration * Appetite problems * Trouble sleeping Postpartum depression symptoms Postpartum depression may be mistaken for baby blues at first — but the symptoms are more intense and last longer. These may eventually interfere with your ability to care for your baby and handle other daily tasks. Symptoms usually develop within the first few weeks after giving birth. But they may begin earlier — during pregnancy — or later — up to a year after birth. Postpartum depression symptoms may include: * Depressed mood or severe mood swings * Crying too much * Difficulty bonding with your baby * Withdrawing from family and friends * Loss of appetite or eating much more than usual * Inability to sleep, called insomnia, or sleeping too much * Overwhelming tiredness or loss of energy * Less interest and pleasure in activities you used to enjoy * Intense irritability and anger * Fear that you're not a good mother * Hopelessness * Feelings of worthlessness, shame, guilt or inadequacy * Reduced ability to think clearly, concentrate or make decisions * Restlessness * Severe anxiety and panic attacks * Thoughts of harming yourself or your baby * Recurring thoughts of death or suicide Untreated, postpartum depression may last for many months or longer. Postpartum psychosis With postpartum psychosis — a rare condition that usually develops within the first week after delivery — the symptoms are severe. Symptoms may include: * Feeling confused and lost * Having obsessive thoughts about your baby * Hallucinating and having delusions * Having sleep problems * Having too much energy and feeling upset * Feeling paranoid * Making attempts to harm yourself or your baby Postpartum psychosis may lead to life-threatening thoughts or behaviors and requires immediate treatment. Postpartum depression in the other parent Studies show that new fathers can experience postpartum depression, too. They may feel sad, tired, overwhelmed, anxious, or have changes in their usual eating and sleeping patterns. These are the same symptoms that mothers with postpartum depression experience. Fathers who are young, have a history of depression, experience relationship problems or are struggling financially are most at risk of postpartum depression. Postpartum depression in fathers — sometimes called paternal postpartum depression — can have the same negative effect on partner relationships and child development as postpartum depression in mothers can. If you're a partner of a new mother and are having symptoms of depression or anxiety during your partner's pregnancy or after your child's birth, talk to your health care provider. Similar treatments and supports provided to mothers with postpartum depression can help treat postpartum depression in the other parent. When to see a doctor If you're feeling depressed after your baby's birth, you may be reluctant or embarrassed to admit it. But if you experience any symptoms of postpartum baby blues or postpartum depression, call your primary health care provider or your obstetrician or gynecologist and schedule an appointment. If you have symptoms that suggest you may have postpartum psychosis, get help immediately. It's important to call your provider as soon as possible if the symptoms of depression have any of these features: * Don't fade after two weeks. * Are getting worse. * Make it hard for you to care for your baby. * Make it hard to complete everyday tasks. * Include thoughts of harming yourself or your baby. If you have suicidal thoughts If at any point you have thoughts of harming yourself or your baby, immediately seek help from your partner or loved ones in taking care of your baby. Call 911 or your local emergency assistance number to get help. Branch report: treatment options and what to expect if help is sought

Postpartum depression is typically treated with a combination of psychotherapy, medication, or both, with evidence suggesting that early intervention can improve outcomes [N4-R4]. The Mayo Clinic source notes that treatment may vary depending on how severe the depression is and what the individual needs, and that recovery time can vary accordingly [N2-F1]. The same source emphasizes that treatment often includes psychotherapy (talk therapy or mental health counseling), with examples such as cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) and interpersonal psychotherapy [N4-R5]. It also states that antidepressants may be recommended, and that most antidepressants can be used during breastfeeding with little risk to the baby, though the provider should weigh the risks and benefits for specific medicines [N2-F1]. The source further notes that other medicines may be added if needed, such as antianxiety medicines for severe anxiety or insomnia, and that Brexanolone is the first FDA-approved drug specifically for postpartum depression in adult women [N2-F1]. It also highlights that with appropriate treatment, symptoms usually improve, but postpartum depression can continue and become long term in some cases [N2-F1].

Nonpharmacologic treatments are central to the evidence base. The Mayo Clinic guidance explicitly names psychotherapy as a first-line option and describes it as helping with coping, problem-solving, goal-setting, and responding to situations more positively [N2-F1]. It also mentions family or relationship therapy as sometimes helpful [N2-F1]. The ABCT fact sheet similarly states that postpartum depression and anxiety can be effectively treated with CBT and/or medication [N4-R5]. The Cleveland Clinic source adds that postpartum depression can last until one year after the child is born, but it does not mean one should feel “cured” in one year, reinforcing the need for sustained support [N5-R4]. Taken together, the evidence supports counseling, support networks, and structured therapy as core treatment options.

For breastfeeding safety, the evidence is more cautious than definitive. The Mayo Clinic source says most antidepressants can be used during breastfeeding with little risk, but it also says the provider should weigh the potential risks and benefits of specific antidepressants [N2-F1]. It also notes that some medicines may be added temporarily if needed, and that Brexanolone is administered in a hospital setting with monitoring because of serious side effects [N2-F1]. The evidence therefore supports that breastfeeding is possible with many treatments, but not automatically safe without provider review [N2-F1]. This matters because the patient may be concerned about the impact of treatment on caregiving and infant feeding.

Recovery is described as variable. The Mayo Clinic source states that treatment and recovery time depend on severity and individual needs, and that symptoms usually improve with appropriate treatment [N2-F1]. It also warns that stopping treatment too early may lead to relapse and that some cases can become chronic depression [N2-F1]. The Cleveland Clinic source notes that postpartum depression can last until one year after birth, but that this does not mean one should feel “cured” in one year [N5-R4]. This means recovery is often not abrupt or short-lived. The evidence also suggests that early intervention can help, including screening during the first week postpartum and routine follow-up visits [N7-R2], [N7-R3]. Overall, the branch report concludes that treatment is likely to include counseling or therapy, may include medication with breastfeeding safety review, and that recovery is usually gradual and may require ongoing care rather than a quick fix [N2-F1], [N4-R5], [N5-R4].

Branch report: what postpartum depression is and how it differs from normal postpartum changes

Postpartum depression is best understood as a mood disorder that occurs after childbirth and is marked by persistent feelings of sadness, anxiety, and fatigue that interfere with caring for the baby or oneself [N1-R3]. The Mayo Clinic source says it is often treated with psychotherapy, medicine, or both, and that it is a health condition that can be treated with medication and therapy [N2-F1]. The Cleveland Clinic source similarly defines it as depression that starts after giving birth and notes that it can include sadness, anxiety, and negative thoughts [N5-R4]. The StatPearls source describes perinatal depression as a mood disorder affecting individuals during pregnancy or within 1 year after childbirth, and the JOGC source adds that a major depressive episode requires at least five symptoms, one of which must be depressed mood or loss of interest [N1-R2], [N1-R4]. While the evidence does not provide a direct DSM-5 definition in the excerpted text, the closest available evidence indicates that postpartum depression is diagnosed using standard mood-disorder criteria rather than being treated as a vague postpartum state [N1-R4].

The key distinction from normal postpartum changes is that postpartum blues are temporary and less severe, whereas postpartum depression is more persistent and disabling. The Mayo Clinic source explains that baby blues are common and usually fade within a few days to 1 to 2 weeks, while postpartum depression is a more severe, long-lasting form of depression [N2-F1]. The same source says that baby blues may include mood swings, crying spells, anxiety, and difficulty sleeping, but that postpartum depression symptoms are more intense and may eventually interfere with caring for the baby and daily tasks [N2-F1]. The Mayo Clinic excerpt also notes that baby blues may begin within the first 2 to 3 days after delivery and may last for up to two weeks [N3-F2]. The Cleveland Clinic source similarly says that most new moms experience baby blues after childbirth, which commonly include mood swings, crying spells, anxiety, and difficulty sleeping, while postpartum depression is a more severe, long-lasting form of depression [N5-R4]. Another source states that baby blues are common, affecting about 70 to 80 percent of new mothers, and that postpartum depression affects around 1 in 8 people who gives birth [N5-R3]. These sources together show a clear pattern: baby blues are short-lived and mild, while postpartum depression is longer-lasting and clinically significant.

The evidence also indicates that symptoms can persist beyond typical postpartum blues and may become concerning. The Mayo Clinic source says that untreated postpartum depression may last for many months or longer and warns that symptoms that do not fade after two weeks, get worse, or make it hard to care for the baby or complete everyday tasks are especially worrisome [N2-F1]. It also notes that symptoms may begin earlier during pregnancy or later up to a year after birth [N3-F2]. The Cleveland Clinic source says postpartum depression can last until one year after birth, but that this does not mean one should feel “cured” in one year [N5-R4]. The NIH excerpt adds that about 5% of women reported persistently high levels of postpartum depression symptoms for three years after giving birth [N6-R5]. Together, these sources indicate that symptoms may persist beyond the first few weeks and may be concerning if they do not improve, worsen, or interfere with daily life.

In summary, postpartum depression is a clinically significant mood disorder that can occur during pregnancy or within one year after childbirth, with symptoms that are more intense and longer-lasting than postpartum blues [N1-R2], [N1-R4]. Normal postpartum blues are brief and common, usually fading within days to weeks, while postpartum depression is more severe, persistent, and likely to interfere with caregiving and daily functioning [N2-F1], [N3-F2], [N5-R4]. The evidence suggests that symptoms may persist beyond the typical postpartum period and become especially concerning if they do not fade, worsen, or disrupt life [N2-F1], [N5-R4], [N6-R5].

## 1) What postpartum depression is, and how it differs from normal postpartum changes

Postpartum depression is best understood as a **mood disorder that occurs after childbirth**, marked by persistent feelings of sadness, anxiety, and fatigue that can interfere with caring for the baby or oneself [N1-R3]. The evidence also shows that it is often treated with psychotherapy, medicine, or both, and that it is a treatable health condition [N2-F1], [N5-R4].

The key difference from **normal postpartum blues** is that **blues are temporary and less severe**, while **postpartum depression is more persistent and disabling** [N2-F1], [N3-F2], [N5-R4]. Normal postpartum blues are common and usually fade within a few days to 1 to 2 weeks, often including mood swings, crying spells, anxiety, and difficulty sleeping [N2-F1], [N3-F2]. In contrast, postpartum depression symptoms are more intense and may eventually interfere with daily life and caregiving [N2-F1], [N5-R4].

The evidence also indicates that symptoms can persist beyond the typical postpartum blues and may even last until one year after birth in some cases, though this does not mean one should feel “cured” in one year [N5-R4]. In addition, about 5% of women reported persistently high levels of postpartum depression symptoms for three years after giving birth [N6-R5]. So, if your symptoms do **not fade after a couple of weeks**, they are more likely to represent postpartum depression rather than ordinary postpartum changes [N2-F1], [N3-F2].

---

The evidence gives clear thresholds for when to seek help. If symptoms do **not fade after two weeks**, get **worse**, or make it hard to care for the baby or complete everyday tasks, help should be sought [N2-F1]. If symptoms include thoughts of harming yourself or your baby, help should be obtained **immediately** [N2-F1]. The Cleveland Clinic source agrees that if symptoms are present and do not fade after two weeks, get worse, or interfere with caregiving, an appointment should be scheduled [N3-F2].

The branch reports also emphasize that **symptoms that are especially worrisome** include those that persist, worsen, or threaten safety [N2-F1], [N3-F2]. These are not just emotional problems; they can signal a more serious condition that needs urgent attention [N2-F1], [N3-F2]. In other words, **do not wait for symptoms to get worse before acting** [N2-F1], [N3-F2].

---

## 3) How long this usually lasts and what to expect

The duration evidence is broad but informative. The evidence suggests that postpartum depression can **last for many months or longer**, and in some cases may persist for **years** [N2-F1], [N6-R5]. Some people may experience symptoms until one year after birth, but this does not mean the condition is resolved in one year [N5-R4]. The NIH excerpt also reports that about 5% of women had persistently high levels of symptoms for three years after giving birth [N6-R5].

So, the patient’s question — “Not sure how long this usually lasts” — has a direct answer: **it can vary, but the usual pattern is that symptoms may last months or longer, and in some cases they may persist for years** [N2-F1], [N5-R4], [N6-R5]. That means **waiting alone is unlikely to make it go away quickly** [N2-F1], [N3-F2].

The evidence-based treatment options are clear. Postpartum depression is typically treated with a combination of **psychotherapy, medication, or both**, with evidence that early intervention can improve outcomes [N4-R4], [N2-F1]. The evidence says that treatment and recovery time depend on severity and individual needs, and that symptoms usually improve with appropriate treatment [N2-F1]. The evidence supports acting early rather than waiting passively [N2-F1], [N7-R2], [N7-R3]. - If symptoms do **not fade after two weeks**
- If they **get worse**

- If you have **thoughts of harming yourself or your baby**

- With appropriate treatment, symptoms usually improve, but stopping treatment too early may lead to **relapse** [N2-F1]

If you are feeling really down all the time after childbirth, the evidence supports that **this is a sign that help may be needed rather than something that will simply go away on its own** [N2-F1], [N3-F2]. The safest and most practical path is to **seek help promptly** if the symptoms are persistent, worsening, or interfering with your life, and to **not wait for symptoms to get worse before acting** [N2-F1], [N3-F2].
